source.title: Safety Arithmetic: A Framework for Test-time Safety Alignment of Language Models by Steering Parameters and Activations
source.authors: Rima Hazra; Sayan Layek; Somnath Banerjee; Soujanya Poria

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present. Some equations and tables are flattened or garbled in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates a safety defense for base, fine-tuned, and edited models. It does not test the listed claims about fine-tuning-induced safety loss, token-position concentration, bypassing opening tokens, localized safety weights, causes of shallowness, or deepening safety.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASR results for its own HDR/Safety Arithmetic method and comparison methods. Those results do not measure any listed claim version. It also reports ASR changes after ROME editing; these bear on harmful behavior after editing, not on the listed fine-tuning or token-depth versions, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. Do not treat its harmful-data fine-tuning to construct a harm vector as a test of whether fine-tuning itself removes safety: the paper does not report that model’s harmful-response rate.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes and evaluates a training-free defense, Safety Arithmetic (harm-vector subtraction plus an in-context safety vector). Its ASR tables measure the defense against baselines. It runs no controlled before/after fine-tuning comparison, no per-token analysis, no prefill, suffix or decoding attack, no localization test, and no deepening training. The harm-vector model θH is fine-tuned on harmful NicheHazardQA answers, but its ASR is never reported. The ROME-edit results concern single-instance knowledge editing, not fine-tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Safety Arithmetic lowers ASR across base, SFT and edited models, preserves utility, and reduces over-safety; Mistral's refusal rate rises slightly.
record.recipe_differences: The source claims concern safety loss after fine-tuning and concentration of alignment effects near response openings. This paper instead constructs a harmful-task vector, prunes and subtracts its parameters, and adds an in-context safety vector at inference time. It also evaluates ROME-edited models.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that changing the top-k fraction affects both ASR and MMLU; it selects 10%. It also reports that the source of exemplars for the in-context safety vector changes the measured ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: A single ROME edit on Llama2-7b-chat raises GPT-4-judged ASR above the unedited model. Unintentional (benign-content) edits: HarmfulQA 23.99→25.18, NicheHazardQA 31.55→38.43. Intentional (harmful) edits: 23.99→26.83 and 31.55→46.91.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-instance knowledge editing (ROME), even with benign content, can increase harmful-response rates in aligned models.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper states that each edited model is produced using a single edit instance. The evaluations use GPT-4 as the ASR judge, report no uncertainty estimates, and describe no hyperparameter search. Experiments cover models up to 7 billion parameters. The extracted tables have some flattened layout.
record.rows_left_out: ASR values for HDR, Safe-Align, Safety Arithmetic, ORTHO, and other comparison methods are omitted because they report the performance of the paper’s defense or attack setup, not an outcome for any listed claim version. SFT-model ASRs likewise do not provide a before-and-after fine-tuning comparison. See Tables 1–3 and 8–13.

untested.parts: No ASR is reported for θH, the model fine-tuned on harmful NicheHazardQA answers. No harmful fine-tuning is compared before and after.
The SFT models are third-party checkpoints with no matched pre-fine-tuning comparison set up by the paper. Benign fine-tuning is not tested.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding bypass. ORTHO is a weight-orthogonalization attack, used only to test the defense.
Top-10% magnitude pruning of the harm vector is a design choice, judged mainly by MMLU and ASR of the defense. It is not a test of whether safety is localized.
Causes of shallowness are not examined.
No training that deepens alignment beyond the first tokens.

record.verdict_notes: Rows R1–R4 are correctly linked to no version. Their 'partial' state is not meaningful without a version: R1 is a near-negligible rise (about 1.2 points), while R4 is a large rise (about 15 points). Table 2 shows the SFT models (e.g. LlamaMath, AdvBench 56.73) with much higher ASR than Llama2-chat (19.81). The paper does not establish a matched backbone or frame this as fine-tuning-induced loss, so it is not treated as a V2 test. Some later studies cite LlamaMath from Bhardwaj et al. 2024 as a chat-model fine-tune, but that is outside this paper. ASR is judged by GPT-4, with no uncertainty estimates and no hyperparameter search.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples makes a safety-trained model comply.
Does not compare benign fine-tuning against the same aligned model before fine-tuning to measure a rise in harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence or its distribution across response positions.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses. Its ORTHO attack results do not test these interventions.
Top-k pruning of a harm vector is used as part of a defense; the paper does not test whether a small set of parameters or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether training data or objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Does not train or evaluate safety spread across response positions or whether deepening safety holds up.
